newsitem.title: USA: Hurricane Danny edges towards a second Gulf Coast landfall.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Danny edges towards a second Gulf Coast landfall.

text.p: Hurricane Danny lashed the U.S. coastline from Mississippi to the Florida Panhandle with squalls and torrential rains on Saturday, as it crept towards a second landfall along the Gulf of Mexico.
The storm's slow but erratic path led the National Weather Service to shift hurricane warnings eastward to Apalachicola, Fla., and cancel earlier warnings west of Gulfport, Mississippi.

At least two people died as the hurricane approached. An elderly man succumbed to a heart attack while securing his boat against rising waters in Pirate's Cove, Alaabama. Another man was found dead in a swamped sailboat near Fort Morgan.

A minimal hurricane packing sustained winds of 75 mph (120 km) and a storm surge up to 5 feet (1.5 metres) above normal, Danny made its first landfall early on Friday in Louisiana between Grand Isle and the mouth of the Mississippi River before moving back into the Gulf on a lumbering northeasterly track.
The storm was expected to come ashore again early on Saturday near Alabama's border with Florida.

At 10 p.m. CDT (11 p.m. EDT), the National Weather Service said the eye of the storm was 50 miles (80 km) southwest of Pensacola, Fla., edging east-by-northeast at 6 mph. Hurricane force winds extended about 25 miles (40 km) from the centre, with the strongest gusts on the east side of the storm.

High winds caused sporadic power outages and threatened to spawn tornadoes throughout the region. A sea-going tornado, known as a water spout, damaged boats and tore roofs off buildings in a marina near Orange Beach, Alabama, late on Friday. No injuries were reported.
The U.S. Coast Guard pulled a stranded surfer out of 8-10 foot seas off Panama City, Florida, on Friday, while rescuers in Mississippi saved two men whose boat capsized near Biloxi.

But officials said the biggest worry was flash-flooding near rivers, streams and saturated lowlands. Weather forecasts called for up to 20 inches of rain along the storm's track over the course of the weekend.
"There's going to be a lot of wind. But our primary concern is rainfall due to its slow movement," said David Eversole, who heads the National Weather Service office in Mobile.

Many coastal residents, long accustomed to more powerful storms, chose to ride out the hurricane and spent all day Friday loading up on batteries and other household goods or nailing sheets of plywood over their windows.
One Alabama resident spray-painted his boarded-up home with the defiant message, "Danny is a Wanna-be."

But others, including thousands of vacationers from the area's surrounding resorts, joined long lines at gas stations before venturing into a steady stream of traffic headed for inland hotels and Red Cross shelters.
"We're staying," said Vicki Bruce, a tourist from Lexington, Kentucky. "There's more danger getting hurt in a traffic jam than there is from this storm."
The governors of Mississippi and Alabama each declared a state of emergency, while authorities in southern Alabama issued a voluntary evacuation of low-lying coastal areas.
All but one of the 11 floating casinos moored along the Mississippi coastline kept their doors open to a trickle of diehard gamblers and tourists.
"It's a little slower than normal, but it's been consistent all day," observed Lori Hutzler, spokeswoman for the Isle Capri Casino in Biloxi, which is open 24 hours a day.
"Patrons went out to get their supplies and then came back to gamble," she said.

Earlier on Friday, high winds, steady rain and wind-driven water bombarded Plaquemines Parish southeast of New Orleans. About 100 boats were damaged or sunk at a large marina in Buras, La., where storm waters rose 4-5 feet (1.2 to 1.5 metres) within a few minutes. In nearby areas, house trailers were overturned, roofs blown off and trees and utility poles snapped, he said.
The crew of the fishing boat Nasty Two rode out the storm in the captain's house of their partially sunken boat after rescuing two other fisherman from a sinking boat in the Empire deepwater canal.

West of Plaquemines, officials in Grand Isle, Louisiana's only inhabited barrier island, reported heavy damage and erosion. Most of the island's 1,530 residents obeyed a mandatory evacuation order Thursday and moved inland.
